claims.text: Premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by size-dependent surface segregation.
Surface segregation creates local compositional fluctuations.
Surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements such as Cu reduces local melting temperatures.
Regions enriched in lower-melting-point elements trigger early, heterogeneous melting.
The initial nanoparticles are solid and compositionally homogeneous, with a random distribution of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu atoms.
Increasing temperature causes atoms with lower cohesive energies, such as Cu, to migrate preferentially to the nanoparticle surface.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller nanoparticles amplifies surface segregation.
Segregation-induced local melting-point depression causes surface premelting that propagates inward.
Smaller nanoparticles have a lower-temperature and broader melting transition than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier and more pronounced onset of premelting than larger nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles in which diffusion is constrained and significant surface segregation does not develop will melt more like a uniform bulk material.
The proposed mechanism applies approximately over the 2–30 nm size range when surface effects are significant and atomic mobility permits diffusion.
Kinetic barriers that prevent segregation can invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Extreme strain or high defect densities can overwhelm the proposed size and segregation effects.
The identity of the dominant segregating element and its quantitative effect on local melting temperature may depend on simulation parameters and processing history.
